Two Relations, One Table →

One-to-Many Relations

A customer's tickets: a foreign key column, plus the relation field Prisma uses to load it.

A customer submits many tickets — the same 1:M shape you already built in Laravel with belongsTo/hasMany. Figure 2.6 shows the Ticket side of it.

// Figure 2.6: a foreign key relation (prisma/schema.prisma, excerpt)
model Ticket {
  id         Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
  subject    String
  customerId Int

  customer User @relation(fields: [customerId], references: [id])
}

customerId Int is the actual foreign key column MySQL stores — no different in principle from a Laravel migration's $table->foreignId('customer_id'). The customer field underneath it is new: it's not a column at all, but a relation field — Prisma's equivalent of Eloquent's belongsTo() method. It tells the generated client "a Ticket's customer is the User whose id matches this row's customerId", which is what makes prisma.ticket.findMany({ include: { customer: true } }) possible later — fetching a ticket and its customer in one call, without writing the join yourself.

On the User side, the reverse relation is a field like tickets Ticket[] — an array, since one customer has many tickets. The real User model actually needs two separate fields like this, which is exactly what the next slide is about.
